newsitem.title: UK: Cancer, heart charities welcome tobacco agreement.
newsitem.headline: Cancer, heart charities welcome tobacco agreement.

text.p: Cancer and heart disease experts on Friday strongly welcomed the surprise admission by U.S. tobacco company Liggett Group that smoking is dangerous and addictive.

In an agreement with 22 state attorneys general who have sued the industry to recoup the Medicaid health care costs of treating smokers, Liggett will allow its employees to testify against other tobacco companies.

"This is the beginning of the end of 40 years of deception," said Richard Peto of the Imperial Cancer Research Fund, who will testify as chief scientific witness in the first case, to be heard in Mississippi next June.
"In 1957 the British Medical Research Council publicly accepted that smoking causes lung cancer, but the tobacco industry have never done so until now," Peto added.
"The truth is about half the cigarette smokers in Britain will be killed by tobacco unless they can get out of their addiction."
Martin Jarvis, the ICRF's addiction expert, predicted an immediate effect on other tobacco companies.
"The rest of the tobacco industry will now find it much harder to maintain their position of denial," he said.

"The acknowledgement both that nicotine is addictive and that tobacco companies have been targeting children as young as 14 shows just how right the FDA (Food and Drug Administration) in the USA was to insist on regulation of tobacco on the grounds that nicotine addiction is a paediatric disease."
Some of the health charities were suspicious.

"Liggett's move is likely to be motivated by cynical business calculations rather than a miraculous conversion to decent civilised behaviour," said John Moore-Gillon, chairman of the British Lung Federation.
"But whatever the reasons, this is a great step forward for people damaged by smoking and for the millions of children not yet hooked on the habit."

The British Medical Association also expressed concern about young people. "At last the tobacco industry is being forced to come clean about its marketing tactics. Today's young people are being cynically exploited and their future health endangered," said BMA chairman Sandy Macara.

He warned that bigger tobacco companies might continue their battle. "Ligget is a relative minnow in the tobacco industry. We can be sure that the tobacco giants will spend billions defending their market and their profits. We cannot allow them to go unchallenged."
Jean King, head of education for the Cancer Research Campaign said she hoped such "aggressive, almost bully-boy tactics" would now end.

"We hope it will signal a change of heart by other leading brand manufacturers, including BAT and Philip Morris, who will inevitably now also have to concede that smoking is addictive and causes cancer."
